transcript.said:
Northshore Dental, a two-chair practice in North Vancouver, BC. Open Mon-Fri 8:00-17:00,
closed Sundays and BC statutory holidays. English only.

The customer comes to us — nobody goes out. Two dentists (Dr. Amy Shen, Dr. Raj Patel)
and two chairs; a booking needs a dentist and a chair free at the same time.

Money. A new-patient exam with X-rays is CAD 180, flat. A recall check-up is CAD 95. An
emergency same-day slot carries a CAD 60 surcharge on top of whatever the treatment costs.
Anything beyond an exam is quoted by the dentist after they have looked — we never quote
treatment over chat. Cancelling or moving with more than 24 hours' notice is free; inside
24 hours we charge CAD 50, and we do say so when they book.

What we will not do:
  - under-16s: we do not treat children, we refer them out and that is a decline
  - anything cosmetic-only (whitening, veneers) — we do not offer it
  - we do not accept walk-ins; everything is booked

Decisions a person must always make: whether something is an emergency worth a same-day
slot is the dentist's call, not the agent's — but the patient says how much pain they are
in and we take that at face value and pass it on. Any question about whether insurance
covers something goes to reception, never answered by the agent.

Who work goes to: the practice manager, Wendy, on Telegram. She confirms attendance and
whether the appointment happened.

After: 24 hours after an appointment somebody checks with Wendy that the patient came and
what was done. If they did not come, the ticket stays open and we chase.

Flow, roughly:
  greet -> get phone -> known patient?
    new -> take name, date of birth, email, and whether they have dental insurance
    known -> is this about treatment we already did? -> yes: hand to Wendy
  then: under 16? -> decline and refer out
        cosmetic only? -> decline
  then: what is wrong / what do they want
  then: is it urgent (their words, not ours)?
        urgent -> tell them the same-day surcharge, hand to Wendy to find a slot today
        not urgent -> offer the next free times, they pick, book it, text them,
                      tell Wendy, arrange the 24h follow-up
transcript.replied:
Read the kit — it's the on-site set (addresses, one technician, travelling diary), so the in-store side will need its own calendar and notify tools. That's next phase.

Your brief covers most of what I'd normally have to ask: hours, both exam prices, the same-day surcharge, the 24-hour cancellation fee, the three declines, who decides what, Wendy on Telegram, and the 24-hour check-back. Two things I can't get from it, both being things a patient will actually hear:

**1. The two declines — how do you say them, and where do the under-16s go?**

For a parent messaging about their 12-year-old, do you name somewhere — a specific pediatric practice in North Van you send people to, a number — or is it "your family doctor can refer you"? I'd like the sentence roughly as Wendy or reception would say it, because the agent will repeat it almost word for word. Same for whitening and veneers: is that "we don't offer cosmetic dentistry" full stop, or is there a softer version, given some of those people are otherwise perfectly good patients?

**2. Someone in a lot of pain, messaging at 3pm on a Tuesday.**

The agent tells them about the CAD 60 surcharge and passes it to Wendy. What does it say to them *while* Wendy is finding a slot — is there a "Wendy will message you within X" promise you'd want made?

And the harder half: is there anything the agent should tell them to do right now, or send them somewhere else entirely? Facial swelling, trouble swallowing, a tooth knocked clean out, bleeding that won't stop — do you have a line you give for those, like go to Lions Gate emergency, or is that not the agent's business at all? I'd rather have your words than invent dental advice.

transcript.said:
1. Under-16s — reception says it like this:

   "We only see patients 16 and over, so we're not able to book your daughter in. North
   Shore Kids Dentistry on Lonsdale takes new patients — 604-555-0142 — and your family
   doctor can refer as well."

   Cosmetic — softer, because these are often good patients otherwise:

   "We're a general practice, so we don't do whitening or veneers. If you'd like a
   check-up or there's anything bothering you, we'd be glad to see you."

2. While Wendy is finding a slot: "Wendy will message you within the hour."

   And yes, there is a line for the bad ones, and it matters more than the booking:

   "If you have swelling in your face or neck, trouble swallowing or breathing, or
   bleeding that won't stop, please go to Lions Gate Hospital emergency now — that's
   past what we can help with from here."

   Knocked-out adult tooth: "Keep the tooth in milk or your own saliva, don't scrub it,
   and get to us or an emergency dentist within the hour — that hour matters."

   Give the safety line whenever any of those is described, whether or not they call it
   urgent. It is not conditional on them asking.

That's everything. Go ahead and plan it.
transcript.replied:
I have enough to design this.

Recorded, in your words, for the rules files and `business_rules.yaml`:

- the under-16 decline, with North Shore Kids Dentistry on Lonsdale, 604-555-0142, and the family-doctor route
- the cosmetic decline, with the "we'd be glad to see you" ending, so it lands as a redirect and not a door closing
- "Wendy will message you within the hour"
- the Lions Gate emergency line and the knocked-out-tooth line — and the important part, that these are **unconditional on the patient calling it urgent**. Whoever hears the symptom gives the line. That is not the urgency step's job, because the description usually arrives before anyone asks how bad it is.

Two small facts I'll assume unless you say otherwise — both are numbers that will end up in `business_rules.yaml`, so I'd rather flag than invent:

- **Saturdays.** You said Mon–Fri 8:00–17:00 and closed Sundays, which leaves Saturday unstated. I'll treat it as closed.
- **The dentist.** I'll let the calendar pick whichever of Dr. Shen or Dr. Patel has a chair free, and record who it turned out to be. If a returning patient should go back to the dentist they saw last time, that's a different booking rule and I need to know before I write it.

Stopping here — the design is the next phase and you get to approve it separately.

transcript.said: Saturday closed is right. Any free dentist is fine — record who it was. Write the plan.
transcript.replied:
`PLAN.md` is written — nothing else. The shape of it:

**17 nodes, 7 of them endings.** Three handovers to Wendy (same-day, treatment question, scheduling), two declines, `no_number`, and `book`.

Three places I did something other than what your sketch says, each called out in the plan:

- **Cosmetic is decided after "what do you want", not before.** You only know it's whitening because they told you. The age gate stays where you put it; the cosmetic gate hangs off the routing that follows intake.
- **The safety line gets a node whose only other job is listening.** Hearing the problem, giving the Lions Gate line, and deciding cosmetic-or-not is three jobs in one prompt, and the one that gets dropped is the one with no tool call forcing it. So `what_for` listens and gives the line; `care_route` decides. The `urgency` node carries the safety tool too, because "how bad is it" is the other place swelling gets mentioned.
- **Insurance has no node.** The question arrives anywhere, so giving every branching node an `insurance` way out would double the graph to model one sentence and a ticket field. It goes in this project's `always.md`, and Wendy sees it because every path to her carries the ticket.

**Eight tools written, eight from the kit.** Two of the written ones exist because the preset is quietly wrong for you: `free_slots` skips Sundays only, so it would offer Saturdays, and its holiday check compares a date to a dict so it never matches one. And `calendar.create_appointment` always picks the first technician and wants a street address.

The rule I'm most pleased to have made code rather than prose: **`diary.book` returns the 24-hour change policy in its own result.** You said you always tell them at booking — this way the node can't put anything in the diary without being handed the fee to say.

**Eight open questions at the end.** The one I'd most like answered is the first: there's a CAD 50 fee for moving inside 24 hours, so patients plainly do move appointments, but there's no path for it in your sketch and none in this plan. When someone asks to move Thursday, do we touch the diary or does Wendy?

Suite is running (13 scenarios, 10 in parallel). While it finishes, the state of things:

**Written and loading clean** — `business_rules.yaml`, `flow.yaml` (17 nodes), `always.md`, `tools/dental.py` (8 tools), 19 rules files, 13 scenarios. The loader has no complaints.

**The tools were exercised directly against a real world before spending a single model call**, which caught two things the graph could not: a 16:30 booking that finished half an hour after the door locks (I was comparing hours, not minutes, against closing time), and confirmation that the roster reduces to Wendy alone so the day-after chase reaches her rather than the simulator's default plumber.

**The first real run failed on two things, both fixed:**
- `book` ended on "I've got your appointment booked. Let me finalize everything" — no time, no dentist, no notice period. `book.md` now spells out the four things the closing message carries, since it is the message they read in the car.
- `urgency` said "we'll get you booked into the next normal appointment" from a node with no diary. That is the promise nothing can keep, so it is now called out by name.

Re-ran after those: clean, 14 turns, no faults.

I'll report the full suite when it lands.
